common_name: Kodiak Red Diervilla (Colorful Native Bush Honeysuckle for Shade)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained to moist soil in partial shade to full sun; Kodiak Red colors up more intensely with some afternoon shade in hot Gulf South summers, making it a useful native alternative to non-native shade shrubs.

directions: Kodiak Red is a hybrid bush honeysuckle selected for foliage that emerges burgundy-red in spring, holds a rich green through summer, and turns deep wine-red again in fall, all on a tough native-derived shrub that spreads slowly by suckers to form a low, dense colony. Small tubular yellow flowers appear in early summer and continue sporadically, drawing bees, but the shrub is grown mainly for season-long colored foliage in spots too shady for most reblooming shrubs. It tolerates dry shade, clay soil, heat, and humidity better than many broadleaf shrubs, asking only for an occasional light shearing in late winter to keep it dense. Use it as a low hedge, bank cover, or woodland-edge planting where its suckering habit is an asset rather than a nuisance.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Kodiak Orange Diervilla (Orange-Red Fall Color Bush Honeysuckle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained to moist soil in partial shade to full sun; give some afternoon shade in the Deep South to prevent leaf scorch in peak summer heat.

directions: Kodiak Orange is a sibling selection to Kodiak Red in the same hybrid bush honeysuckle line, distinguished by orange-tinted new growth in spring that shifts to green in summer and then to vivid orange-red in fall, giving two distinct color seasons on one tough, suckering native-derived shrub. Small yellow tubular flowers open in early summer and sporadically after, attracting bees and providing a minor nectar source in shaded beds where flowering shrubs are scarce. It handles dry shade, heat, humidity, and average garden soil with little complaint, and a light shearing in late winter is usually all the maintenance it needs. Its slow-spreading habit makes it useful for erosion control on shaded slopes or as a colorful low border along a woodland edge.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Kodiak Black Diervilla (Dark Purple-Black Foliage Bush Honeysuckle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained to moist soil in partial shade to full sun; foliage color develops darkest with a few hours of direct sun rather than in deep shade.

directions: Kodiak Black carries the darkest foliage of the Kodiak bush honeysuckle series, emerging deep burgundy-purple and holding that near-black color through the growing season before a final flush of red in fall, giving strong dark-foliage contrast in shaded beds that otherwise lean heavily on green. Clusters of small yellow tubular flowers appear in early summer and draw bees, though the shrub's main appeal is season-long colored foliage rather than a big floral display. Like its Kodiak siblings it is a tough, suckering, native-derived shrub that tolerates dry shade, clay, heat, and humidity, and needs only an occasional light shearing to stay dense. Pair it with chartreuse or silver-leaved shade perennials for strong color contrast in a partly shaded border.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Yuki Cherry Blossom Deutzia (Groundcover Pink-Flowered Deutzia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; its low, spreading habit suits it to mass planting, a border edge, or a large container.

directions: Yuki Cherry Blossom is a true dwarf, groundcover-habit selection of slender deutzia bred from the same low-mounding line as Chardonnay Pearls, covering itself in small, star-shaped flowers that open pale pink and hold their color better than most deutzia, which usually fade quickly to white. Its compact, spreading form stays under 2 feet tall while spreading wider, making it useful as a flowering groundcover, edging plant, or mass planting rather than a typical upright specimen shrub. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and prune lightly right after flowering if a tidier shape is wanted, since it blooms on the previous year's wood. It is otherwise low-maintenance and rarely troubled by pests or disease.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Sonic Bloom Red Weigela (Reblooming Red-Flowered Weigela)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; light deadheading of the first spring flush helps trigger the summer and fall rebloom cycles.

directions: Sonic Bloom Red is the red-flowered member of the Sonic Bloom weigela series, bred to rebloom on new growth through summer and into fall rather than flowering only in a single spring flush like older weigela cultivars. Trumpet-shaped, deep red-pink flowers open heavily in mid-spring and then continue sporadically for months, drawing hummingbirds well past the usual short weigela bloom window. Give it full sun for the strongest rebloom, well-drained soil, and only light shaping right after the main spring flush, since heavy pruning removes the wood that carries the later flushes. It is otherwise a tough, adaptable shrub that tolerates heat, humidity, and average garden soil with little fuss.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Double Play Doozie Spirea (Reblooming Deep Pink Compact Spirea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; shear off the first spent flush to encourage the summer and fall rebloom typical of the Double Play series.

directions: Double Play Doozie bears the deepest, most saturated raspberry-pink flower clusters in the compact Double Play spirea series, opening in late spring and rebooming through summer into fall on new growth after a light shearing of the spent flowers. Its tight, mounded habit stays under 2 feet tall, fitting easily into small foundation beds, mixed borders, or mass plantings where larger old-fashioned spireas would need constant cutting back. New foliage emerges with a reddish tint before turning blue-green for summer, adding a second color feature besides the flowers. It is drought-tolerant and low-maintenance once established, needing only a late-winter cutback to remove old wood and keep the shape tidy.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Zydeco Twist Okra (AAS-Winning Spineless Spiral-Podded Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed following the last frost, since okra seed germinates slowly and unevenly in cold soil; soaking seed overnight speeds emergence.

directions: Zydeco Twist was an All-America Selections regional winner recognized for pods that spiral and twist rather than growing straight, a shape that lets the pods stay tender and stringless a few days longer than most straight-podded types before they turn woody. The plant is compact and spineless, with no itchy prickles on the pods or foliage, making harvest far more comfortable than on older bristly okra varieties. Sow directly in warm soil after the last frost in full sun, and pick pods every day or two once production starts, since okra quickly overshoots the tender stage in hot weather. Its shorter, well-branched habit fits into smaller garden beds better than tall heirloom okra varieties while still producing heavily through the heat of summer.
